front.title: Anamnesis: Event Records for the Unheaded Protocol

abstract.t: This document specifies Anamnesis, the event log of the Unheaded Protocol. BPF programs that process packets carrying a Monad register write fixed 32-octet event records into ring buffers on the host where they run, without blocking the packet path. The document defines the record format, the rules for producers and consumers, and how records are correlated into a trace. Event Type values are registered by the Unheaded Protocol Foundation; this document creates no registry.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Unheaded Protocol Foundation carries a 20-octet Monad register in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option . The programs that insert, process and strip that register run as BPF programs attached to the network path. Anamnesis is how they report what they did: each program writes an event record when a packet is born at a Shield, crosses a hop, is changed by the chaos subsystem, fails a check, or leaves the Kingdom.
Anamnesis has three properties that the rest of this document preserves:

list.t: It never slows the packet. A producer that cannot write a record drops the record, not the packet, and never waits.
It carries metadata only. A record holds a timestamp, an Event Type, a hop identifier, part of the flow label and a copy of the Monad register. It never holds packet payload.
It is local. Records stay on the host that produced them. A host agent may forward what it reads (for example to Wotan ), but the 32-octet record is not a wire format and is never placed in a packet.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dd.t: A BPF program that writes event records.
A BPF ring buffer (BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF) owned by one producer program, into which it writes event records.
A host process that reads records from one or more rings.

section.name: Event Record Format

dd.t: Nanoseconds from the producing host's monotonic clock at the time of the event, in the producing host's native byte order. Timestamps from different hosts are not comparable.
A value from the "Unheaded Anamnesis Event Types" registry .
The identifier of the hop that emitted the record, as configured on that hop.
The low 16 bits of the packet's IPv6 Flow Label , in network byte order.
The 20-octet Monad register as it stood when the event occurred, in the octet order of the wire format .

section.t: A producer MUST write all 32 octets of every record it commits. A record has no padding and no field that is left unwritten.

section.name: Event Types
section.t: The Event Type octet takes its value from the "Unheaded Anamnesis Event Types" registry created by . This document does not repeat that registry and assigns no value.

Some producers emit EVENT_COMPUTED records larger than 32 octets, for example the cartridge trace records of . Those records begin with the Event Type octet followed by a Sub-kind octet, are carried on a stream separate from the rings of this document, and are governed by the "EVENT_COMPUTED Sub-kinds" rules and registry in . A consumer of 32-octet records MUST NOT interpret any octet of such a record as a Sub-kind.

list.t: MUST NOT block, retry or loop while reserving space in a ring. If the reservation fails, the producer MUST drop the record and SHOULD increment a drop counter that a consumer can read.
MUST NOT copy packet payload octets into a record or into any other field it emits to Anamnesis.
MUST emit a record at every hop for a packet whose Monad TRACED flag is set , subject to rule 1.
SHOULD size its ring from the expected event rate, the record size and the longest interval a consumer may fall behind, so that drops are rare in normal operation.
MUST discard a record that is not exactly 32 octets long.
MUST count and discard a record whose Event Type it does not recognize, and MUST continue reading the ring. An unknown Event Type is not an error of the ring.
MUST NOT assume that the Monad snapshot carries a valid checksum: an EVENT_ANOMALY record may report exactly the packet whose checksum failed.
SHOULD expose the drop counters of the producers it reads, so that a gap in a trace can be told apart from a quiet flow.

section.name: Correlating Records into a Trace
section.t: Records that belong to the same packet's journey share the trace ID in their Monad snapshots ; the Flow Label bits narrow the search when trace IDs are reused. Within one host, timestamps order the records. Across hosts, ordering comes from the hop sequence (birth, hops, death) and from the Monad hop count, not from timestamps.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Anamnesis records carry flow metadata. The Monad snapshot holds service identifiers, a trace ID, QoS and flow-action values and flags; the Flow Label bits identify a flow. No record carries payload (producer rule 2), and no field holds a key or a credential. Access to the rings MUST be limited to the host agents that need them, since a reader learns which services talk to which and when.

A producer that overflows its ring loses records, not packets. An attacker who floods a hop can therefore blind tracing for that hop but cannot use Anamnesis to stall the data path. Consumers SHOULD alert on drop counters for this reason.

Records are written by BPF programs and read by host processes. A consumer MUST treat every field as untrusted input: a record may describe a malformed packet, and the Event Type may be one the consumer does not know (consumer rule 2).
Producer rule 2 and the requirement to write all 32 octets together keep kernel memory and packet payload out of the log.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. The registries it uses (Anamnesis Event Types and EVENT_COMPUTED Sub-kinds) are created by .

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
This document specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6). It obsoletes RFC 2460.

This document specifies the IPv6 Flow Label field and the minimum requirements for IPv6 nodes labeling flows, IPv6 nodes forwarding labeled packets, and flow state establishment methods. Even when mentioned as examples of possible uses of the flow labeling, more detailed requirements for specific use cases are out of the scope for this document.
The usage of the Flow Label field enables efficient IPv6 flow classification based only on IPv6 main header fields in fixed positions. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

eBPF (which is no longer an acronym for anything), also commonly referred to as BPF, is a technology with origins in the Linux kernel that can run untrusted programs in a privileged context such as an operating system kernel. This document specifies the BPF instruction set architecture (ISA).

section.t: The record format follows the implementation in the Unheaded repository (ebpf/monad-common, pkg/protocol/bpfschema), whose size and offset tests fix it at 32 octets.
